name: Text to SQL Benchmarks
title: Text to SQL Benchmarks
answer: Text to SQL benchmarks are standard test sets that measure how well a system turns a plain language question into a working SQL query. Public benchmarks such as Spider and BIRD score text to SQL systems by running the generated query and comparing its result with a known correct answer. They matter because they give teams a common yardstick for comparing models, prompts and retrieval setups on the same questions. Enterprise schemas are larger and less tidy than the benchmarks, so real accuracy is usually lower. The gap between a leaderboard score and a working query against a production warehouse is the central fact of this topic.

sections.body: Text to SQL benchmarks are standard test sets that measure how well a system turns a plain language question into a working SQL query. They matter because they give teams a common yardstick for comparing models, prompts and retrieval setups on the same questions. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Running a benchmark means standing up a database per example, loading the schema and seed rows, then executing whatever SQL the system produces. That usually happens in a container or a throwaway cloud instance so a bad query cannot touch anything real. The harness needs a SQL engine, a driver, a way to capture result sets and errors, and a store for the questions, gold queries and gold answers. Because every page on this site is itself built from a PostgreSQL database, the same engine that serves the site can serve as the execution target for benchmark runs. Larger suites add scheduling and parallelism so thousands of questions finish in reasonable time.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core method is execution accuracy: run the generated query, compare its result set with the result of the reference query, and count a match. Some suites also report exact match against the gold SQL string, which is stricter and punishes correct queries written differently. Harder variants test robustness to paraphrased questions, unseen schemas, and cross database transfer, where a system is trained on one set of schemas and evaluated on another. Error analysis usually separates syntax failures, wrong joins, wrong filters and right answer by luck. Teams read the per question breakdown more than the headline number, because it shows which failure mode to fix next.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Benchmark data carries its own provenance questions. Spider and BIRD are research artifacts with their own licences and citation expectations, and redistributing them inside a commercial evaluation pipeline is a decision someone has to make deliberately. Enterprise evaluation is harder still, because the schemas, column names and sample rows may be confidential, so teams often build private question sets and keep the gold queries internal. Any evaluation that touches real data needs the same access controls as the warehouse itself, including masking and audit logging. A benchmark score is evidence about a system, not a guarantee about a deployment, and it should never be presented as one.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is away from single clean questions and toward messy, multi table, multi step tasks that look more like real analyst work. Expect more benchmarks that grade the whole interaction, including clarification questions, follow up corrections and the ability to say a question cannot be answered from the available schema. Agentic setups that inspect a schema, draft a query, run it, read the error and revise are already changing what a good score means. As text to SQL moves into production reporting, the interesting metrics will shift from exact match toward whether a human reviewer accepts the answer and how often the query needs repair.
